deep.reconstruction:
OVERVIEW. The page continues the table begun on the previous folio. For primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4), running downward from 1117 to 929 (plus supplements for 1873 and 2609), it lists the cycles of reduced binary quadratic forms of determinant p, in Gauss's sense b^2 − ac = p. This is equivalent to the continued-fraction expansion of √p. It also tallies how many classes such forms have for the primes 4n+1 between 1000 and 2000.

(A) PRINCIPAL CYCLES.
Notation (the recurrence is my modern restatement):
- P_0 = 0, Q_0 = 1, a_k = floor((√p + P_k)/Q_k).
- P_{k+1} = a_k Q_k − P_k.
- Q_{k+1} = (p − P_{k+1}^2)/Q_k.
Each line '1.Q1.Q2. ...' is the sequence of Q_k, i.e. the outer coefficients of the successive reduced forms (±Q_k, P_{k+1}, ∓Q_{k+1}) of determinant p.

Example, p = 1109 (my check):
- √1109 ≈ 33.30, so P1 = 33 and Q1 = 1109 − 1089 = 20.
- a1 = 3, P2 = 27, Q2 = 380/20 = 19.
- a2 = 3, P3 = 30, Q3 = 209/19 = 11.
- a3 = 5, P4 = 25, Q4 = 484/11 = 44.
- This continues 17, 5, 4, 37, 29, 20, 41, 13, 25, 25.

Because p ≡ 1 (mod 4) is prime, the period is odd and symmetric. Gauss stops ('&c.') where two equal consecutive Q's appear (Q_k = Q_{k+1} = q). At that point the form (q, P, −q) has p = P^2 + q^2, so the table also yields the representation of p as a sum of two squares. All instances on the page check:
- 1117 = 26²+21²; 1109 = 22²+25²; 1097 = 16²+29²; 1093 = 2²+33².
- 1069 = 30²+13²; 1061 = 10²+31²; 1049 = 32²+5²; 1033 = 32²+3².
- 1021 = 30²+11²; 1013 = 22²+23²; 1009 = 28²+15².
- 997 = 6²+31²; 977 = 4²+31²; 953 = 28²+13²; 941 = 10²+29².
- 937 = 24²+19²; 929 = 20²+23²; and in the supplement 1873 = 28²+33².
The first terms check directly as well, e.g. 1117 − 33² = 28, 1873 − 43² = 24, 1097 − 33² = 8.

(B) NON-PRINCIPAL CYCLES.
When the class number exceeds 1, further cycles are listed, starting from small values (3, 4, 9, 27):
- 1093: cycles beginning 3 and 9.
- 1009: cycles beginning 3, 9 and 27.
- 997: a cycle beginning 4, e.g. the form (4, 31, −9), since 31² + 36 = 997.
Each non-ambiguous cycle stands for a class together with its opposite. The class number is therefore 1 + 2 × (number of extra cycles): 1093 → 5, 1009 → 7, 1129 (previous page, 4 extra cycles) → 9.

(C) 'Rec.' (recensio). 'Inter 1000 & 2000 sunt 67 numeri primi formae 4n+1'.
Distribution of class numbers:
- 51 primes have 1 class.
- 9 have 3: 1213, 1229, 1301, 1373, 1489, 1613, 1861, 1949, plus the later-added 1973.
- 2 have 5: 1093, 1429.
- 2 have 7: 1009, 1601.
- 2 have 9: 1129, 1901.
- 1 has 11: 1297.
The counts add up: 51+9+2+2+2+1 = 67. All class numbers are odd, as genus theory requires for a prime determinant ≡ 1 mod 4. This matches the earlier lines (1213 and 1229 have one extra cycle each; 1297 has five). It also agrees with known minimal cases from the following page (401 → 5, 577 → 7).

(D) 'Suppl. 2609. 84'. This is a different computation, for the NEGATIVE determinant −2609 (positive forms (a,b,c) with b² − ac = −2609).
- 2609 is prime, and −2609 ≡ 1 (mod 3), so (3,1,870) exists.
- Row k gives the reduced form (a,b) in the class (3,1,870)^k. Examples:
  - k=1: (3,1,870)
  - k=2: (9,1,290)
  - k=3: (27,19,110)
  - k=4: (33,8,81)
  - k=5: (11,8,243)
  - k=6: (33,19,90)
  - k=7: (30,11,91)
  - k=8: (10,1,261)
  - k=9: (30,1,87)
  - k=10: (29,28,117)
  - … up to k=24: (42,25,77)
- From k=27 on, Gauss writes only the leading coefficients: 51, 17, 51, 26, …, 45, 15, 5, 15, 45, 22, …, 18, 6, 2 (b for 3 values).
- At k = 42 he reaches (2,1,1305), which is ambiguous (2b = a). So (3,1,870)^42 lies in an ambiguous non-principal class, and (3,1,870) has order 84 — the '84' at the head of the column.
- The symmetric patterns of a (33, 11, 33 around k=5; 45, 15, 5, 15, 45 around k=34; 18, 6, 2, 6, … around k=42) are the expected signature: if C^m = F_q, then C^{m±1} = F_q·C^{∓1} has a = 3q.
- Since the genus count gives just 2 ambiguous classes, the 2-part is cyclic. The page shows a class of order 84, i.e. a large cyclic (sub)group for this determinant.

Purpose. These are Gauss's class-number tables for prime positive determinants (Disq. Arith. arts. 187, 303–304 context), with the side product p = x² + y². There is also a test computation of the order of a class for a negative determinant with a large class number.
errors: 2609 table, row 25: '27.17' cannot be correct as written. 17² + 2609 = 2898 is not divisible by 27; b must be ≡ ±8 (mod 27), e.g. 19 or 8. This is either a slip (17 for 19) or a misreading.
Rows 26, 31, 38, 39 of the 2609 table are left blank, and from row 27 on only leading coefficients are recorded. The table is incomplete, but this is not wrong.
No errors detected in the spot-checked continued-fraction sequences; all terminal pairs satisfy p = P² + q².

results.what: Periods of the continued fraction of sqrt(p) (principal cycles of reduced forms of determinant p) for primes p ≡ 1 mod 4, 929–1117 and 1873.
results.modern_name: Continued fraction expansion of sqrt(p) / cycle of reduced indefinite binary quadratic forms
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1770s), Legendre; Gauss Disq. Arith. art. 183ff

results.what: Reading off p = x² + y² at the symmetric midpoint of the odd period.
results.modern_name: Legendre/Gauss continued-fraction method for sum of two squares (cf. Cornacchia, Smith)

results.what: Class numbers of forms of prime determinant p ≡ 1 mod 4 for 1000 < p < 2000: 51 with h=1, 9 with h=3, 2 with h=5, 2 with h=7, 2 with h=9, 1 (1297) with h=11.
results.modern_name: Class number tables for real quadratic fields / positive determinants (Cohen–Lenstra-type statistics)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's Nachlass tables (Werke II); later Cayley, Ince, etc.

results.what: Powers of the class (3,1,870) of determinant −2609, showing it has order 84 (its 42nd power is the ambiguous class (2,1,1305)).
results.modern_name: Computing the order of an element in the class group of discriminant −4·2609
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (composition of forms, Disq. Arith. art. 305–307)

deep.surprise_reason: This is Gauss's known class-number table work for positive determinants, which survives in his Nachlass and was published in Werke II, plus routine continued-fraction computations. The −2609 cyclic-order computation is a nice unpublished worked example but fits his known interests (Disq. art. 306).
